questions.problem:
Which of the following random variables could be modeled by an exponential distribution?

I. The execution time, in seconds, of a computer program

II. The number of students in a class with blood type $A$

III. The number of books read by a student in a month
questions.worked_solution:
The exponential distribution can be thought of as the continuous analog of the geometric distribution. It models the amount of continuous time or space until a particular event occurs, where the events should occur independently and at a constant average rate.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable I could be modeled using an exponential distribution. Executions of a computer program can be modeled as independent events with a constant average rate, and we wish to know the amount of time it takes to complete a single execution.

- Random variable II does *not* follow an exponential distribution. There are no events that occur at a constant average rate, and there is no interval of continuous time or space. The number of students is discrete, not continuous.

- Random variable III does *not* follow an exponential distribution. There is no interval of continuous time or space. The number of books is discrete, not continuous.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem: The lifetime of a certain type of electrical switch varies continuously. Lifetime of different switches of this type are independent, and switches replacements have a constant average rate of one every $2$ years. Determine the probability that a switch fails between the first and the second year. Round your answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the lifetime of the switches varies continuously, lifetimes of different switches are independent, and switches replacements have a constant average rate, we can model the lifetime of a switch using the exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the lifetime, in years, of a random electrical switch. The lifetime can be modeled as an exponential random variable. Since switches are replaced every $2$ years on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{2},$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{2}).
$$

In this case, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that a switch fails between the first and the second year is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X<2) & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =-{e}^{-1}+{e}^{-1/2} \\  & ≈0.2387\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the time until the next error. The time until the next error can be modeled as an exponential random variable. Since errors occur once every $30$ days on average, the rate is $\lambda =1/30,$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{30}).

 In this case, $X$ has the following probability density function:

questions.problem: The arrivals of vehicles at a crossing occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of one every $10$ seconds. Determine the probability that the next vehicle will arrive at the crossing at least $5$ seconds after the previous vehicle's arrival. Round your answer to four decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Since arrivals of vehicles at the crossing occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next vehicle arrives as an exponential distribution.

An exponential random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ be the amount of time between the arrival of two successive vehicles at the crossing. Then, since vehicles arrive every $10$ seconds on average, the rate is $\lambda =\frac{1}{10}$ vehicles per second.

The time between arrivals can be modeled as an exponential random variable with rate $\lambda =\frac{1}{10},$ and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{10}).
$$

So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the next vehicle will arrive at the crossing at least $5$ seconds after the previous vehicle's arrival is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & ={\int }_{5}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{\infty }\frac{1}{10}{e}^{-x/10}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{e}^{-x/10}{|}_{5}^{\infty } \\  & =-{e}^{-\infty }+{e}^{-5/10} \\  & =0+{e}^{-1/2} \\  & ={e}^{-1/2} \\  & ≈0.6065.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Emails arrive in a professor's inbox continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $2$ emails per day. If the professor has not received an email for the past $3$ days, what is the probability that an email will arrive in the next $2$ days? Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

The required probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since emails arrive continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next email using the exponential distribution.

Let $X$ represent the time, in days, until the next email arrives. Given that emails arrive at an average rate of $2$ per day, the rate parameter is $\lambda =2$ emails per day, and we can write 

$$
X∼\text{Exp}(2).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. Therefore, given two positive real numbers $s,t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.
$$

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$
P(X\le s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=1-{e}^{-\lambda t}
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda =2,$ $s=3,$ and $t=2.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3+2\,|\,X>3) & =P(X\le 2) \\  & =1-{e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & =1-{e}^{-(2)(2)} \\  & =1-{e}^{-4} \\  & ≈0.982.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P(X>s+t\,|\,X>s)=P(X>t)={e}^{-\lambda t}.

We can compute the complementary conditional probability as follows:

$$

canonical_examples.problem: A malfunctioning internet server approves connection requests continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $2$ requests per minute. If a user has been waiting for $30$ seconds to connect, what is the probability that they will have to wait at least $20$ more seconds?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since connection request approval occurs continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next request is approved using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the user's waiting time in seconds. Since the server approves $2$ requests per minute on average (or $1$ request every $30$ seconds), the rate is $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{30}$ requests per second, and we can write

$$
X\sim \textrm{Exp} \left( \dfrac{1}{30} \right).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s, t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{30},$ $s=30,$ and $t=20.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>30+20\,|\,X>30) & =P(X>20) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/30)\cdot (20)} \\  & ={e}^{-2/3} \\  & ≈0.513.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **Poisson process** is a mathematical model used to describe events occurring randomly over continuous space or time. A Poisson process is characterized by the following properties:

- Events occur *independently*. In other words, one event's occurrence does not affect another event's likelihood.

- Events occur at a *constant average rate*. The rate at which events occur represents the expected number of events per unit of time or space.

tutorials.name: Modeling Using the Memoryless Property
tutorials.problem:
The memoryless property of the exponential distribution states that the probability of an event occurring in the future is independent of the time already passed. 

For a random variable $X$, the probability that the event occurs in the next $t$ units of time, given it hasn't occurred after $s$ units of elapsed time, is

$$
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

Suppose you have a radioactive particle whose decay time $X$ follows the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda = 0.8 \text{ decays/minute}.$

Then, the probability that the particle will decay in the first minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0.8{e}^{-0.8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={-{e}^{-0.8x}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-{e}^{-0.8}+{e}^{0} \\  & =1-{e}^{-0.8} \\  & ≈0.5507.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose the particle doesn't decay in the first minute. What is the probability that it will decay in the next minute? We can answer this question using the memoryless property.

By the memoryless property, we have

$$
P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

Taking the complement of this event, we have

$$
P(X < s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = P(X < t) = 1-e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have that $s=1$ and $t=1,$ so

$$
P(X < 1+1 \, \big|\, X>1) = P(X < 1) \approx 0.5507
$$

In other words, even if the particle has survived for one minute, the probability that it will decay in the next minute remains the same as at the start of the observations.

steps.title: Identifying Situations That Can Be Modeled Using an Exponential Distribution
steps.html:
Example: Identifying Situations That Can Be Modeled Using an Exponential Distribution
?

Which of the following random variables could be modeled by an exponential distribution?

  1. The time interval between successive arrivals of customers in a store
  2. The number of customers in a store at a particular time
  3. The weight of a child at birth
EXPLANATION

The exponential distribution can be thought of as the continuous analog of the geometric distribution. It models the amount of continuous time or space until a particular event occurs, where the events should occur independently and at a constant average rate.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

  • Random variable I could be modeled using an exponential distribution. Customer arrivals can be modeled as independent events with a constant average rate, and we wish to know the amount of time until the next customer enters the store.

  • Random variable II does not follow an exponential distribution. There is no interval of continuous time or space. The number of customers in a store is discrete, not continuous.

  • Random variable III does not follow an exponential distribution. There are no events that occur at a constant average rate.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
